Internal 
From Policy to Action: IFRC Supports Eswatini's New 
Disaster Risk Management Authority Through 
Anticipatory Action Initiatives 
 
Figure 1: Launch of the National Disaster Risk Management Authority in the Kingdom of Eswatini 
The Government of Eswatini has officially launched the National Disaster Risk 
Management Authority (NDRMA) on 28 April 2026 marking the transition from the former 
National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) and a major shift in the country’s 
approach to disasters. This move signals a deliberate departure from a predominantly 
response‑oriented system towards a forward ‑looking, risk ‑informed and anticipatory 
framework. It reflects growing recognition that disasters are not isolated emergencies, 
but predictable and manageable risks that require sustained preparedness, early action, 
and long‑term resilience building. 
The NDRMA is established under the National Disaster Risk Management Act of 2025, 
which provides a strengthened legal and institutional basis for disaster risk governance 
in Eswatini. While the NDMA played a vital role in coordinating disaster response and 
recovery, escalating climate ‑related hazards, socio ‑economic vulnerabilities, and 
recurrent shocks highlighted the need for a more comprehensive mandate. 
The revised Act expands the authority’s responsibilities beyond emergency response to 
include disaster risk reduction, preparedness, anticipatory action, and resilience building. 
Launched by the Deputy Prime Minister Thulisile Dladla, the NDRMA represents a 
significant reform aimed at ensuring that disaster risk is addressed proactively and
Internal 
systematically, in support of sustainable development and the protection of vulnerable 
communities. 
This step positions Eswatini among a growing number of countries in Southern Africa 
demonstrating leadership in proactive disaster risk management. 
A Risk Context That Demands Anticipation 
Eswatini’s disaster risk profile underscores the urgency and importance of this transition. 
The country is exposed to a range of hydrometeorological hazards, including recurrent 
droughts, flooding, severe storms and strong winds. These hazards intersect with 
structural vulnerabilities, including reliance on rain -fed agriculture, pockets of poverty, 
and exposure of informal settlements. As a result, disasters in Eswatini often have 
disproportionate impacts on women, children, rural communities, and people depending 
on subsistence livelihoods. 
Historically, responses to these shocks have been largely reactive, mobilizing resources 
after impacts have already occurred. While lifesaving, such approaches are costly and 
insufficient in the face of increasingly predictable climate hazards. The launch of the 
NDRMA represents a strategic shift to act earlier, smarter, and based on risk and the 
Deputy Prime Minister Dladla emphasized at the launch that “The authority must 
strengthen early warning systems so that timely and reliable information reaches all 
communities, including rural and vulnerable populations. It must ensure that disaster risk 
reduction is integrated into development planning, so that p ublic investments are protected 
and future risks are reduced”. 
From Management to Risk Governance 
The evolution from the NDMA to the NDRMA reflects a deeper transformation in how 
disaster risk is understood and governed. Under the previous framework, disaster 
management was primarily centered on coordination of response, often triggered once 
impacts were already visible, but the National Disaster Risk Management Act broadens 
this scope by elevating disaster risk reduction and preparedness as core national 
priorities, embedding anticipatory action, enabling early responses based on forecasts, 
triggers, and risk analysis, promoting multi-sectoral coordination, linking climate, water, 
agriculture, health, social protection, and infrastructure planning and s upporting 
resilience building at community, institutional, and systems levels. 
By institutionalizing these functions within the NDRMA, Eswatini is creating the legal and 
operational space to invest before crises escalate, reducing humanitarian needs and 
safeguarding development gains. 
Creating an Enabling Environment for Anticipatory Action 
The launch of the NDRMA is particularly significant in the context of anticipatory action, 
This new authority provides a stronger foundation for linking early warning systems with 
early action protocols, s caling forecast -based financing and pre -agreed response 
mechanisms, s trengthening collaboration between national institutions, traditional 
structures, civil society, and international partners and b ridging humanitarian action, 
disaster risk reduction, and climate adaptation
Internal 
In a country where droughts and floods are increasingly predictable, anticipatory action 
has the potential to protect lives, livelihoods, and public resources, while reinforcing 
national ownership of disaster risk decisions. 
Translating Policy into Early Action 
The IFRC commends Eswatini for this forward-looking reform and looks forward to seeing 
how the NDRMA advances anticipatory action, reduces disaster losses, and strengthens 
resilience for all EmaSwati. 
The establishment of the NDRMA creates significant opportunities for Baphalali Eswatini 
Red Cross Society, supported by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red 
Crescent Societies (IFRC), to further advance anticipatory action in Eswatini. With an active 
Drought Early Action Protocol, a Flood simplified Early Action Protocol under 
development, its strong community presence, volunteer network, and experience in early 
action, livelihoods support, and disaster preparedness, Baphalali is well positioned to 
support the operationalization of anticipatory action at local level linking national early 
warning systems to community ‑based early action, targeting the most vulnerable 
households before shocks escalate. Through IFRC’s global expertise in forecast ‑based 
financing, early action protocols, and risk ‑informed programming, the Red Cross 
(Baphalali Eswatini Red Cross Society, IFRC, British Red Cross Society and Red Cross Red 
Crescent Climate Centre are already supporting the NDRMA in scaling anticipatory action 
mechanisms, strengthening risk analysis, developing pre‑agreed triggers, and promoting 
coordination across sectors. This partnership offers a pathway to translate policy into 
practice, ensuring that anticipatory action delivers timely, people‑centered and locally led 
protection of lives and livelihoods in the face of recurrent climate hazards. 
A Commendable Step Forward 
The launch of the National Disaster Risk Management Authority is more than an 
institutional rebranding, it is a signal of intent, the Deputy Prime Minister Dladla 
explained that “This transition is not only symbolic. It represents a significant change in the 
way Government intends to manage disaster risk. The country is moving from a system that 
was largely associated with disaster response to a stronger and more proactive system focused 
on risk reduction, preparedness, early warning, response, and recovery” . It reflects political 
commitment to protecting people not only when disasters occur, but before they unfold. 
As climate risks intensify across Southern Africa, Eswatini’s proactive stance offers an 
encouraging example of how countries can move beyond response, embrace 
anticipation, and invest in resilience as a development priority. Continued success will 
depend on sustained resourcing, strong coordination, community engagement, and the 
effective operationalization of anticipatory and preparedness mechanisms but the 
foundation is now firmly in place. 
Contact: Tawonga.dalikeni@ifrc.org

Accordingly, our respective Governments, through representatives assembled in the city of San Francisco, who have exhibited their full powers found to be in good and due form, have agreed to the present Charter of the United Nations and do hereby establish an international organization to be known as the United Nations.

related.excerpt: A Trump administration official on Sunday grappled with mounting criticism over the length of the US war with Iran after months of promised diplomatic breakthroughs, short-lived ceasefires, and the deaths of two more American troops in Jordan bringing the total number of American military members killed in the conflict to 16. Appearing on ABC’s This Week, US energy secretary Chris Wright defended the Trump administration’s strategy after being confronted with his earlier claims that the war which began in February would have ended by now. Wright argued that the mission has since shifted toward ensuring oil shipments can move through the strait of Hormuz. “We did a pause to try to get an agreement with the Iranian people to allow oil to flow without them attacking it,” Wright said. “They’ve proven unwilling to do that, and we’ve pivoted.
